segments.say: We've seen that procrastination can mean more stress near deadlines, and less sleep at night. But researchers have also wondered about bigger questions. Is procrastination linked to people's wider wellbeing? Their mental health, their physical health, their sense of connection to others?

In two thousand and twenty three, a team of researchers in Sweden, led by Fred Johansson, published a study following about three and a half thousand university students over time. They measured how much the students procrastinated, and then, about nine months later, looked at a range of health and wellbeing outcomes.

show.where: Sophiahemmet University, Sweden, published in JAMA Network Open, 2023
show.what: About 3,500 university students in Sweden were followed over time. Their procrastination was measured, and later their mental health, sleep, physical symptoms and lifestyle.

segments.say: They found that higher levels of procrastination were associated with somewhat worse outcomes later on. Including more symptoms of depression, anxiety and stress, more disabling pain in the upper body, poorer sleep quality, more loneliness, and more financial difficulties. The associations were generally small. But they appeared across many areas of life.

It's important to be careful about what this means. This kind of study shows associations, not proof that procrastination directly causes these problems. It's possible that some of the arrows point both ways. Stress and poor sleep can make us procrastinate more, and procrastination can make stress and poor sleep worse. Real life is full of such loops.

But the study adds to a picture we've been building all night. Procrastination isn't just about missed deadlines. It's tangled up with how we feel, how we sleep, and how we cope with stress. And that's actually a hopeful message, because it means that working on procrastination can bring benefits far beyond productivity.

If you reduce procrastination a little, you might also reduce last minute stress a little. Sleep a bit better. Feel more in control. And if you take care of your sleep, stress and mood, procrastination might become a little easier to manage too. Each small improvement can support the others.

Some psychologists suggest seeing procrastination as a signal. A sign that something about the task, or our situation, or our feelings, needs attention. Maybe the task is unclear. Maybe we're exhausted. Maybe we're afraid. Maybe we're doing something that doesn't truly matter to us. Listening to that signal can be wiser than fighting it.

And I want to add something gently. Sometimes, persistent difficulty starting tasks can be connected to other things. Like depression, which can drain energy and motivation. Or attention difficulties such as ADHD, which can make starting and organizing tasks especially hard. If procrastination feels overwhelming and constant, it's worth talking to a doctor or a psychologist. Help is available.

And whatever the reason, procrastination is not proof that you're lazy, or broken, or a bad person. It's a common human pattern that's tied to emotions, energy and circumstances. Seeing it that way makes it easier to care for yourself, and easier to change.

So perhaps the best way to tackle procrastination isn't only with planners and deadlines, but by caring for the whole person. Sleep. Rest. Connection. Kindness. Meaningful goals. When the person is cared for, the tasks often become easier to face.

So here's what research on wellbeing suggests. Procrastination is linked, modestly, to stress, sleep, mood and other parts of life. These links probably go in both directions. It can help to treat procrastination as a signal, not a verdict on who you are. And if it feels overwhelming, talking to a professional can really help.

show.title: Procrastination and wellbeing
items: It's linked to stress, sleep and mood
The links are small and go both ways
Treat it as a signal, not a verdict
Seek help if it feels overwhelming

segments.say: So far, delay has looked mostly like a problem. But is there ever a good side to putting things off? Some researchers have found that a little delay can sometimes make us more creative. And some people suffer from the opposite problem. Doing things too early. Let's look at both.
